title: Oracy Doesn't Have to Be a Disaster
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles holds two positions that look contradictory: oracy is not a scalable whole-school solution, yet it is the missing link in teaching English literature. He opposes the schoolwide push, announced by England's Education Secretary, because the only provider that tried to scale it, Voice 21, produced no measurable attainment gains in EEF trials and schools found it impossible to roll out. His test is that an idea that is right but cannot be scaled is not credible, and he compares oracy to diet and exercise as a morally right remedy that fails at population level. For English literature he proposes giving students two extreme interpretive questions per text and using speed dating, competing essays, a five-connectives game and drama routines such as hot seating and freeze frames to build rival arguments before they write. The timing rule is essential: talk activities come only after students know the plot, characters and key quotes, otherwise oracy replaces understanding. He concludes that oracy is an approach to exploring knowledge, never a skill to be taught for its own sake, and pairs it with reading whole texts quickly in two to three weeks.
points: Salles rejects oracy as a schoolwide initiative on evidence grounds, noting the EEF found no impact from Voice 21 and that schools could not scale it.
He proposes that oracy suits English literature specifically, where debating two extreme interpretations forces students to form their own view and answer an opponent.
The practical toolkit includes speed-dating debates, competing model essays, a five-connectives game, hot seating, line of conscience and freeze-frame perspective tasks.
Speaking activities must follow, never replace, knowledge of the plot, characters and key quotations, or oracy substitutes for understanding.
Teach each text quickly in big chunks (2-3 weeks), keeping the text rather than the skill as the curriculum, with skills as a byproduct.
quotes: Oracy is the diet and exercise of teaching. It is morally right. It just doesn’t work at scale.
As I’ll never tire of saying, it is not enough to be right. You also have to find a way to make it work.
Another way of putting it is this: if it isn’t scaleable, it isn’t credible.

The first step is simply to ask students to develop a point of view. The trick is to give them two extremes to debate - this forces students to develop their own views, and also forces them to listen to their opponents and respond

If students know only a little, they will have nothing worthwhile to say. The speaking activities are never while you are studying the texts. It is always after studens have learned the plot, understood the characters and analysed key quotes and scenes.
If you don’t do that, oracy will replace understanding. If you think of oracy as a set of skills, as Voice 21 does, you will always go wrong.
It is always an approach to exploring knowledge and ideas. Skills will develop as a natural consequence of the tasks you set. The skill itself is not the task.
The idea is to finish every text within a maximum of 2-3 weeks - 7 to 10 hours of teaching.
